Three documents are on record. Tuvalu's own constitution, adopted in September 2023, declares that its statehood is perpetual. In November 2023 Pacific Islands Forum leaders endorsed a declaration that their members' statehood will continue despite climate change. That same month Australia pledged its support for the continuation of Tuvaluan statehood in a treaty, the Falepili Union, and it offered residency to 280 Tuvaluans a year.

entries_new.pop: Officially four: Barros, his wife and two children
entries_new.currency: The Ponto, replaced by bitcoin in 2015
entries_new.laws: A planned constitution and a citizenship charter
entries_new.name: Principality of Pontinha
entries_new.anchor: Forte de São José on the Ilhéu do Diego, at the southern edge of Funchal, Madeira.
entries_new.stopped_by: Portuguese authorities, who never recognised it; Barros later lost the property through insolvency
entries_new.challenge: About a decade of legal disputes, and an arrest by Portugal's National Guard in 2017
entries_new.recognition: None from Portugal or its regional authorities
entries_new.story:
The Principality of Pontinha is a micronation declared on a small rock at the edge of Funchal, the main city of the Portuguese island of Madeira. The rock, the Ilhéu do Diego, carries the Forte de São José, a fort built around 1760. It was joined to the shore in 1775, and in 1888 or 1889 it was partly demolished and the rubble used for a jetty. It now sits within Funchal's southern seawall.
The claim rests on a sale. The Blandy family, British wine exporters, leased the site and bought it at auction in 1903. In 1999 the Blandys put it up for sale, and Renato Barros, a visual arts teacher, bought it. His price is not known. In January 2007 Barros declared the site independent. He argued from the 1903 sale document that the site had stopped being Portuguese territory when it was sold. He renamed it the Principado do Ilhéu da Pontinha and set its national day on 3 October, a date he associated with that sale.
The argument treats two different things as one. Buying land gives a person ownership of it, under the law of the country where the land lies. The right to rule the land is sovereignty, and a sale of land between private owners or at auction does not normally move that right. A house bought from a town council remains in the same country.
Barros gave the principality a flag, a coat of arms, a citizenship charter and a planned constitution. Its currency, the Ponto, was replaced by bitcoin in 2015, and it had a language called Funcho. He registered himself as the first citizen, and his wife and two children made up the rest of the official population. In 2010 he asked the government's representative in Madeira to detach the site from Portugal.
Neither the national nor the regional authorities recognised it, and about a decade of legal disputes followed. In 2017 Portugal's National Guard arrested Barros for failing to close his premises, and he was released pending trial. How that case ended is not known. He was later declared insolvent and the property was auctioned. A group of Madeirans returned from abroad bought it and planned a museum. As of 2021 the museum had not opened. Barros went on appearing in public as prince and posting on the principality's Facebook page, while the territory itself had passed to other owners under ordinary Portuguese property law.
entries_new.mechanism: Buying a site at auction gives ownership under the law of the country it lies in. It does not move the right to rule, and here the property itself was later sold off through an ordinary Portuguese insolvency.

sources.t: de Castro and Hayward, on the Principality of Pontinha, Transformations issue 35 (2021)

entries_new.laws: Australian law, with a council holding wide powers of local government
entries_new.cost: Estimated at 10 million pounds, around A$274 million today
entries_new.name: Curtis Island offer to the Nauruans
entries_new.anchor: Curtis Island, near Gladstone, Queensland, Australia.
entries_new.founder: Australian government and its partner governments
entries_new.stopped_by: The Nauruans, who refused to go
entries_new.challenge: Refused by the Nauruans; no court was involved
entries_new.recognition: None offered: Australia refused to give up sovereignty
entries_new.story:
Nauru is a very small island in the Pacific, and in the early 1960s it was run jointly by Australia, New Zealand and Britain. For decades those three countries had mined its phosphate, a rock used for fertiliser. Mining damaged the island so badly that scientists judged it would be uninhabitable by the mid-1990s. Repairing the land was considered far too expensive. The government of Australia therefore looked for somewhere to move the whole population. In 1962 Prime Minister Robert Menzies acknowledged a "clear obligation" to provide a satisfactory future for the Nauruans.
Australia looked at sites in Fiji, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands and the Northern Territory, and at Fraser Island. In 1963 it offered Curtis Island, near the town of Gladstone in Queensland. The land was privately held, so the government planned to acquire it and give the Nauruans freehold title, the fullest ordinary form of land ownership. Farming, grazing, fishing and commercial businesses were to be set up. The partner governments would pay for resettlement, including housing and infrastructure, at an estimated 10 million pounds.
The sticking point was the right to rule. Australia refused to give up sovereignty. Nauruans could become Australian citizens and run local affairs through a council with "wide powers of local government", but Curtis Island would stay part of Australia. A people would own the land as a private owner does and would answer to Australian law.
The Nauruans refused. They did not want to be assimilated into White Australia or to lose their identity as a distinct people, and many saw resettlement as a cheap fix compared with repairing their island. The Australian government regarded the offer as generous and said it would not change its position. No one moved. Nauru stayed where it was and became independent in 1968.
The case shows the limit of what buying land can do for a people. A government can pay for an island and hand over title, and the people on it still live inside that government's country unless it agrees to give up the right to rule.
entries_new.mechanism: Freehold title gives a people ownership of land and leaves sovereignty, the right to rule it, with the state. The Nauruans turned the offer down because Australia would give them the first and not the second.

sources.t: How the entire nation of Nauru almost moved to Queensland, The Conversation

entries_new.laws: Section 113 of the constitution of Saint Kitts and Nevis, which allows secession by referendum
entries_new.name: Nevis secession referendum, 1998
entries_new.anchor: Nevis, the smaller island of the federation of Saint Kitts and Nevis, in the Caribbean.
entries_new.stopped_by: The two-thirds majority required by Section 113 of the federal constitution
entries_new.challenge: A lawful vote that fell short, with 61.7 percent in favour against the two-thirds required
entries_new.recognition: Not reached; Nevis stayed in the federation
entries_new.story:
Saint Kitts and Nevis is a Caribbean country made of two islands. Its constitution has a written procedure for one part to leave. Section 113 lets Nevis secede through a referendum, and it requires a two-thirds majority of the vote. That makes the case useful, because the question was settled by counting votes against a known rule.
The islands have been linked on and off since Europeans settled them in the early 17th century. From 1882 they formed a single colonial unit, along with Anguilla, governed from Basseterre on Saint Kitts. In 1970 the ferry M.V. Christena sank with the loss of 223 people, most of them from Nevis, and that disaster became a key event in the rise of the secession movement. The Nevis Reformation Party, formed that same year with secession as its aim, got the clause into the constitution in the early 1980s. The federation became independent in 1983 without Anguilla. An unofficial vote on Nevis in 1977 had been ignored by the central government.
In 1995 the Saint Kitts and Nevis Labour Party returned to power on the federal level. Its plans for a federal office on Nevis and for central control of financial services led the Nevis administration to use the clause. On 10 August 1998 voters on Nevis were asked whether they approved a bill called the Nevis Constitution (Secession) Order, 1998.
The result was 61.7 percent in favour. That is a clear majority, and it failed, because two-thirds is about 66.7 percent. Nevis stayed in the federation. Partisan rivalry on the island has made a second attempt harder to win at that threshold, and no second referendum has been held. Secession has largely left the political agenda, and federal treatment of Nevis has been described as more respectful since 1998.
The Nevis case shows both sides of a written way out. The vote was lawful, and the same document set a threshold high enough that a large majority still lost.
entries_new.mechanism: A constitution can give a region a lawful way to leave and set the terms. Here it required two-thirds of the vote, so 61.7 percent in favour was not enough.

sources.t: Lecours, Saint Kitts and Nevis: Secessionism and the Federal Experience, Forum of Federations policy brief, July 2026

entries_new.pop: About 52,908 (1991 estimate), on about 420 square kilometres
entries_new.currency: Deutsche Mark, US dollar, French franc and pound sterling, and possibly the Yugoslav dinar
entries_new.name: Republic of Western Bosnia
entries_new.anchor: Velika Kladuša, its capital, in north-western Bosnia and Herzegovina.
entries_new.stopped_by: A joint action by Croatian and Bosnian government forces in August 1995
entries_new.challenge: Overrun by Bosnian government forces in 1994, restored with Serb help, and ended in 1995
entries_new.story:
The Republic of Western Bosnia was a small breakaway territory inside Bosnia and Herzegovina during the Bosnian war of the 1990s. Its capital was Velika Kladuša, and it covered about 420 square kilometres, with an estimated 52,908 people in 1991. Its founder was a businessman with a large local employer. Fikret Abdić, nicknamed Babo, founded Agrokomerc, an agricultural company in Velika Kladuša that became Yugoslavia's largest food-processing conglomerate, employing about 13,000 people.
On 27 September 1993 Abdić declared the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia in Velika Kladuša, with himself as president. It had no currency of its own and used several foreign ones. It did not stand alone. It aligned with Serbia, Croatia and the Krajina Serbs, the breakaway Serb territory across the border in Croatia, and Abdić signed non-aggression pacts with Mate Boban and Radovan Karadžić. Its army therefore fought against the Bosnian government, a conflict known as the Intra-Bosnian Muslim War.
The province depended on those neighbours for its survival. In June and August 1994 Bosnian government troops took its territory in Operation Tiger. Serb forces then helped drive them out in Operation Spider, and the province was re-established. On 26 July 1995 it declared itself independent as the Republic of Western Bosnia, a name it used only briefly. By then it served as the last line of defence for the Republic of Serbian Krajina. On 7 August 1995 a joint Croatian and Bosnian government action destroyed it, about twelve days after the declaration, and Abdić fled to Croatia.
No state ever recognised it. Abdić was convicted of war crimes in Croatia and sentenced in 2002 to 20 years. He was released on 9 March 2012, and in 2016 voters in Velika Kladuša elected him mayor.
It held real control on the ground for a time, through pacts with stronger neighbours, and it was overrun both times that it lost their protection.
entries_new.mechanism: A breakaway territory without recognition can hold ground through pacts with stronger neighbours. Here the territory was overrun in 1994 until Serb forces helped restore it, and it ended in 1995 under a joint Croatian and Bosnian government action.

sources.t: Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, Wikipedia
